title: Cafe Membership Note
topic: A pass that does not break even at the full cup price
blurb: A coworker wrote up whether the cafe's monthly pass is worth it.
prompt: A coworker asked an AI to check this cafe-pass note. If a line doesn't add up, tap it.

segments.label: The usual price
segments.text: A latte at the cafe downstairs is $5.

segments.label: The pass
segments.text: The $20 monthly pass gives you 20% off every drink you order that month.

segments.label: The break-even
segments.text: The pass costs the same as four full-price lattes, so anyone who buys more than four coffees a month comes out ahead.

segments.label: The habit check
segments.text: Most people on our floor already grab a morning coffee on at least ten workdays.

segments.label: The suggestion
segments.text: The note recommends buying the pass before the first of the month.

conclusion: AI check: the $20 pass equals four $5 lattes, so more than four drinks a month makes it worth it. Buy the pass.

flaws.original: The pass only saves $1 per $5 latte (20% off), so you need 20 drinks a month — not 4 — to earn back the $20 fee.
flaws.corrupted: The pass costs the same as four full-price lattes, so anyone who buys more than four coffees a month comes out ahead.

diagnosis_choices.label: 20% off a $5 latte only saves $1 per cup — you need 21 cups a month to beat $20, not 5.
Four $5 lattes cost $20, so buying exactly 4 coffees breaks even and you need 5 to profit — wait, $20/4 = 5.
The $20 pass includes 4 free lattes up front, so you actually come out ahead on cup 4, not cup 5.
20% off $5 is $4 per latte, so 5 lattes cost $20 total — you break even at 5, not 4.

fix_choices.label: Divide $20 by the $1 saved per cup: break-even is 20 lattes a month (profit starts at 21).
Divide $20 by the $4 discounted latte price: break-even is 5 lattes, profit starts at 6.
Count the $20 pass as 4 free lattes, so anyone buying 4+ lattes breaks even.
Divide $20 by 20% ($20 × 0.20 = 4) and add 4 cups to get 8 lattes to break even.

flaws.explanation: A discount pass pays itself back at the amount you save per cup, not at the full cup price. $1 off a $5 latte means you need 20 cups, not 4, to earn back $20.
flaws.why_tempting: Matching the pass price to four full $5 cups feels like a break-even point — as if each coffee you buy were a $5 credit against the fee.
flaws.catch_rule: For a paid discount, break-even is fee ÷ amount saved per use, not fee ÷ full price.
flaws.hint: With the pass, how much do you actually save on one $5 latte? How many of those savings add up to $20?

practice.problem: A $30 shop card gives 10% off $6 sandwiches. How many sandwiches to break even?

clean_segments: A latte at the cafe downstairs is $5.
The $20 monthly pass gives you 20% off every drink you order that month.
Each latte then costs $4, a $1 saving, so you need 20 drinks a month to earn back the $20 fee — not 4.
Most people on our floor already grab a morning coffee on at least ten workdays.
Ten drinks a month still leaves you $10 short of breaking even, so the pass is optional, not an obvious win.
clean_conclusion: The pass saves $1 a cup, not $5. You need 20 drinks a month to break even, not 4.

diagnosis: $5 doesn't include tax and tip, so the true cup price is closer to $6 and breaks the break-even math.
Other drinks at the cafe cost $3 or $7, so using a $5 latte misrepresents the pass.
At $5 a latte, 20% off is $1.25 off per cup, not $1.00.
You can't judge the pass from a $5 latte without comparing against brewing coffee at home ($0.50).
fix: Include a $1 tip so each latte is $6 ($1.20 saved per cup).
Average the cafe's whole menu price instead of picking a $5 latte.
Compare the pass against home-brewed coffee before recommending it.
Check whether specialty oat-milk lattes ($6.50) qualify for the 20% off.

diagnosis: 20% off every drink means you pay 20% ($1 per latte), saving $4 a cup.
A $20 monthly pass auto-renews, so one forgotten month doubles the break-even to 8 lattes.
20% off only applies after you spend $20 on full-price drinks first.
The $20 fee is credited toward your first four drinks, so it isn't an extra cost.
fix: Confirm whether the $20 fee is store credit or a pure membership fee.
Check if 20% off has a daily cap of one drink per workday.
Turn off auto-renew so you don't pay $20 during vacation months.
Calculate savings at $4 per cup (80% off) vs $1 per cup (20% off).

diagnosis: 10 workdays a month is only half of the ~20 workdays in a month, so the floor barely drinks coffee.
Saying 'most people' buys at least 10 coffees ignores teammates who only visit the office twice a week.
At 10 lattes a month, you only save $10 on a $20 pass — you actually *lose* $10, not come out ahead.
Ten $5 lattes cost $50, and 20% off $50 is $40, leaving zero profit after the $20 pass.
fix: Count 10 lattes × $1 saved = $10 saved vs $20 pass — a $10 loss, not a win.
Only recommend the pass to people who buy 21+ lattes (nearly every workday).
Check whether hybrid workers really hit 10 workdays in the office.
Survey exact monthly cup counts before recommending the pass to the floor.

diagnosis: Buying before the 1st of the month wastes the remaining days of the current month.
Buying before the 1st doesn't save money if the pass starts a rolling 30-day clock on purchase.
Recommending the pass to 10-coffee drinkers locks them into losing $10 every month.
Waiting until the 2nd of the month lets you see if you even want coffee that week.
fix: Don't buy the pass unless you order 21+ $5 drinks a month; 10-cup drinkers lose $10.
Wait until your first coffee of the new month if the pass runs 30 rolling days.
Try tracking how many coffees you buy next month before signing up.
Share one pass between two 10-cup coworkers if the cafe allows it.
